what_it_does: Rich emollient butter that softens skin and helps reduce moisture loss.
summary_short: Shea butter is mainly a nourishing emollient: it softens rough, dry skin and leaves a protective, cushiony feel. It is usually well tolerated, though very heavy formulas may feel greasy or clog-prone for some acne-prone users.
summary_long:
Shea butter is a plant-derived fat from the nut of the shea tree. In skincare, its main job is **emollience**: filling in tiny gaps between dry, flaky skin cells so the skin feels smoother and more comfortable. Because it is rich in fatty acids such as stearic and oleic acids, it also helps create a light occlusive layer that can reduce water loss from the skin.

It is best supported as a moisturizing and barrier-support ingredient rather than as a treatment for specific skin conditions. Traditional use and cosmetic experience suggest it can be helpful for dryness, rough patches, and compromised-feeling skin, while claims around anti-aging, wound healing, or inflammation are more limited and should be interpreted cautiously.

Shea butter can appear in small amounts in lotions for added richness, or at higher levels in balms, body butters, lip products, hand creams, and barrier creams. Higher concentrations make a formula feel thicker, more cushiony, and more occlusive, which can be helpful for very dry skin but may be too heavy for oily or acne-prone areas.

Most people tolerate shea butter well, and refined grades are less likely to have a strong natural scent. Irritation is uncommon, but botanical ingredients can still bother sensitive users, especially in fragranced formulas. People with acne-prone skin may want to patch test or reserve richer shea-heavy products for the body or dry zones.

Shea butter pairs well with humectants like glycerin or hyaluronic acid, which pull water into the skin, and with barrier-supporting ingredients like ceramides, petrolatum, dimethicone, or plant oils. There are no major routine conflicts, but its rich texture can interfere with layering if used before lighter serums or sunscreen, so it is usually best applied near the end of a routine.
quick_facts: Rich emollient for dry, rough skin
Common in balms and body butters
Can feel heavy on oily skin
Usually best near the end of a routine
